findings.title: Flag allowlist rejects newer/valid RegExp flags (e.g. 'd')
findings.explanation:
The change introduces an allowlist `ALLOWED_FLAGS_RE = /^[gimsuy]*$/` and rejects any flags not in that set during `validatePattern()` (lines added near the top of `customRulesEngine.ts`). Modern JavaScript/Node runtimes support additional RegExp flags (for example the `d` indices flag introduced in newer ECMAScript versions). By hard‑rejecting anything outside `gimsuy`, the validation will incorrectly refuse otherwise valid user regexes that use supported flags (causing valid custom rules to be rejected).

When it occurs: when a user calls `validatePattern()` (or `add_custom_rule`) supplying a flag such as `d` that is supported by the runtime but not included in the allowlist.

Impact: users with existing/valid rules using such flags will see rule validation fail and be unable to add rules; this is a backward‑compatibility regression and may break legitimate workflows. The security intent is valid, but the implementation can cause false rejections.

Suggested fix: either extend the allowlist to include runtime‑supported flags (e.g. add `'d'`), or perform feature detection (e.g., attempt to construct a `RegExp` with the supplied flags and catch errors) rather than relying on a hardcoded character class that may lag language changes.

findings.title: Test imports and jest.mock ordering can cause mock/real binding mismatch
findings.explanation:
The test file imports `fileExists` and `getFileStats` (and `MAX_FILE_SIZE_BYTES`) at the top, then calls `jest.mock('../../utils/fileUtils.js', ...)` later in the same file and casts the imported symbols to `jest.MockedFunction` (lines 1–54). If `jest.mock` is not hoisted (depending on test runner configuration / ESM behavior), the imported bindings may already be bound to the real implementations instead of the mock factories declared in `jest.mock(...)`. That leads to fragile tests or runtime errors when the code later treats those imports as mocked functions.

When it occurs: while running the test suite under environments where `jest.mock` is not hoisted before imports (common in ESM contexts) or when the test runner doesn't apply hoisting for those calls.

Impact: flakey tests or type/assertion failures in CI; tests may exercise real filesystem code unexpectedly.

Suggested fix: move the `jest.mock('../../utils/fileUtils.js', ...)` call to the top of the module (before importing the functions that will be mocked), or avoid importing the functions directly and instead require/import them after mocking, or use `jest.unstable_mockModule` / top-level hoisted mocks appropriate for the environment so the imported bindings point at mocks reliably.
